page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The five configurations
steps.why: Writing each element on its own line with the noble gas core keeps the configuration short and shows the outer shell clearly, which is the part the question is about. In gallium, indium and thallium the filled d and f subshells may be written before or after the ns electrons; both orders are used and both are correct.
common_mistakes: Writing gallium as [Ar]4s²4p¹. The ten 3d electrons are filled before 4p and must be shown.
Leaving out the 4f¹⁴ in thallium. Both the f and the d subshells are complete before 6p.
steps.memory_tip: From gallium onward an inner d shell is filled, and from thallium an f shell as well.
steps.margin_note: Use the noble gas core; the full form is long and easy to get wrong.

steps.label: The general form
lines: Every element of the group has three
Those three electrons are why the group
steps.why: One line, ns²np¹, covers all five elements: two electrons in the s subshell and one in the p subshell of the outermost shell n, which is three valence electrons in every case.
common_mistakes: Writing ns²np³. Group 13 has one p electron in the valence shell, not three.
Counting the filled d electrons as valence electrons. The valence shell is the outermost one, ns²np¹.
steps.memory_tip: Group 13, three valence electrons: two in s and one in p.
steps.margin_note: Write ns²np¹ once; that one line covers all five elements.

insider_note: The five configurations and the general form ns²np¹ both belong on the page, because the general form is the single line that explains the +3 state.
